title: Saying no without saying no
goal: Refuse an invitation, a plate of food or a favour without making anyone lose face, and recognise when an Indonesian is politely refusing you. Along the way, meet *nggak enak*, *sungkan* and *segan* — the feelings that make all this necessary.
bekal: turn down an offer softly: *sebenarnya…*, *kayaknya kurang bisa*, *nanti saya kabari*
explain *nggak enak*, *sungkan* and *segan* and use them about yourself
refuse a friend by offering something else instead: *Gimana kalau aku…?*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Undangan Pak Harun
dialogs.intro: A Thursday evening in early April. After a long day of homestay inspections, Sarah stops at Pak Harun's house to drop off some forms. It is getting dark, and he is not letting her leave that easily.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah, monggo, makan malam di sini saja. Ibu sudah masak sayur asem.
lines.id: Sarah, please, have dinner here. My wife's made sour vegetable soup.
lines.literal: Miss Sarah, please, eat night at here just. Mother already cook vegetable sour.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Aduh, terima kasih, Pak. Sebenarnya saya masih kenyang.
lines.id: Oh, thank you. Actually, I'm still full.
lines.literal: oh-dear, thank you, sir. actually I still full.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Lho, sedikit saja. Nggak enak kalau tamu pulang belum makan.
lines.id: Oh come on, just a little. It doesn't feel right to let a guest go home without eating.
lines.literal: [lho], little just. not pleasant if guest go-home not-yet eat.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kalau begitu, saya coba sedikit, nggih.
lines.id: In that case, I'll try a little, then.
lines.literal: if like-that, I try little, yes.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Nah, gitu. Oh ya, Sabtu malam ada kenduri di rumah adik saya. Mbak ikut, ya?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sabtu, ya, Pak… Kayaknya kurang bisa. Saya sudah janji ke Bu Endang di Yogya.

lines.literal: Saturday, yes, sir… seems less can. I already promise to Mrs Endang in Yogya.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Wah, sayang sekali. Kalau Minggu pagi? Kami mau panen di sawah.
lines.id: Oh, what a pity. How about Sunday morning? We're harvesting in the fields.
lines.literal: wow, pity very. if Sunday morning? we want harvest at rice-field.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Minggu pagi saya belum tahu, Pak. Nanti saya kabari, ya.
lines.id: I don't know about Sunday morning yet. I'll let you know.
lines.literal: Sunday morning I not-yet know, sir. later I inform, yes.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Ya, ya. Jangan sungkan, lho, Mbak. Anggap saja rumah sendiri.
lines.id: Of course. Don't be shy, now. Make yourself at home.
lines.literal: yes, yes. don't reluctant, [lho], Miss. consider just house own.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Justru saya yang sungkan, Pak. Bapak sudah terlalu baik.
lines.id: It's me who feels awkward. You've been far too kind.
lines.literal: precisely I who reluctant, sir. you already too kind.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Ah, biasa saja. Malam ini menginap di sini saja, sudah gelap.
lines.id: Oh, it's nothing. Stay the night here, it's already dark.
lines.literal: ah, ordinary just. night this stay-over at here just, already dark.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih banyak, Pak, tapi besok jam tujuh saya harus di kantor.
lines.id: Thank you so much, but I have to be at the office at seven tomorrow.
lines.literal: thank you many, sir, but tomorrow hour seven I must at office.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Ya sudah. Hati-hati di jalan. Ini, bawa pisang untuk Bu Endang.
lines.id: All right then. Take care on the road. Here, take some bananas for Bu Endang.
lines.literal: yes already. careful at road. this, bring banana for Mrs Endang.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Matur nuwun, Pak. Salam untuk Ibu.
lines.id: Thank you very much. My regards to your wife.
lines.literal: thank you, sir. greeting for Mother.

notes: **Nggak enak** — literally “not tasty” — is the key to this unit. It is the uncomfortable feeling of having imposed on someone, disappointed them, or failed a social duty. Pak Harun feels *nggak enak* letting a guest leave hungry; Sarah will feel *nggak enak* refusing him. Standard: *tidak enak (hati)*.

**Sebenarnya** (“actually, in truth”) is the classic opening of a refusal. It announces that what follows is not quite what you would like to say. *Sebenarnya saya mau, tapi…* — “I'd love to, but…” — is the pattern.

**First refuse, then accept a little.** Food is usually offered more than once, and a first refusal is not taken seriously. Accepting a small amount on the second offer (*saya coba sedikit*) is the graceful way out for both sides.
**Kayaknya kurang bisa** — “it seems I can't quite”. Every word softens: *kayaknya* adds doubt, *kurang* replaces *tidak*. Nobody hears anything but “no”, but nobody is hurt by it either.

**Nanti saya kabari** — “I'll let you know”. Sometimes it means exactly that. Often it is a gentle no that saves both people from saying it now. Listen to the tone, and notice whether the person ever does let you know.

**Monggo, nggih, matur nuwun** — Javanese at home: “please (go ahead)”, “yes”, “thank you very much”. Sarah answers in kind because it pleases him; a foreigner who says *matur nuwun* in a Javanese kitchen gets a smile every time. *Kenduri* (also *selamatan*) is a communal prayer meal.

grammars.title: The soft no: building blocks
body: A polite Indonesian refusal is assembled from a few standard pieces: a sound of regret, a softener, a reason, and a door left open. You rarely need all four, but you nearly always need two.
after: A full example: *Aduh, sebenarnya saya mau sekali, Pak, tapi Sabtu kayaknya kurang bisa. Saya sudah ada acara. Lain kali, ya.* Nobody would call this a long-winded answer in Indonesian.
⚠️ The reason does not have to be important — *sudah ada acara* (“I've got something on”) is accepted everywhere and is rarely questioned. What matters is that you give one.

grammars.title: kurang: “less” that means “not”
body: *Kurang* means “less, lacking”, but in front of an adjective or verb it very often works as a softened *tidak*. It is the most useful politeness tool in this unit.

head: With kurang
English
Blunter version
rows: feeling a bit under the weather

after: *Kurang tahu* is the standard polite way to say “I don't know” to a stranger or an elder; a bare *tidak tahu* can sound dismissive.
The literal meaning is still alive: *sayurnya kurang garam* (the vegetables need more salt), *uangnya kurang* (there isn't enough money). Context makes it obvious which one you mean.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Jadi MC? Aduh…
dialogs.intro: That weekend, in Yogya. Rina calls from Jakarta with a question about her wedding, which is set for late October.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Sar, aku mau minta tolong. Kamu mau nggak jadi MC di resepsiku?
lines.id: Sar, I need a favour. Would you be the MC at my reception?
lines.literal: Sar, I want ask help. you want not become MC at reception-my?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Hah? Aku? Rin, aku terharu banget, tapi sebenarnya aku nggak pede.
lines.id: What? Me? Rin, I'm really touched, but honestly I don't feel confident.
lines.literal: huh? me? Rin, I moved very, but actually I not confident.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Lho, bahasa Indonesiamu udah bagus banget, kok.
lines.id: Come on, your Indonesian's really good.
lines.literal: [lho], language Indonesian-your already good very, [kok].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kalau ngobrol sih bisa. Tapi MC resepsi Jawa kan pakai bahasa Jawa halus.
lines.id: Chatting, sure. But MCs at Javanese receptions use refined Javanese, don't they?
lines.literal: if chat [sih] can. but MC reception Java [kan] use language Java refined.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Iya juga, sih. Keluarga Andi dari Solo semua.
lines.id: That's true, actually. Andi's whole family is from Solo.
lines.literal: yes also, [sih]. family Andi from Solo all.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah. Aku takut salah ngomong di depan eyang-eyangnya Andi.
lines.id: Exactly. I'd be terrified of saying the wrong thing in front of Andi's grandparents.
lines.literal: there. I afraid wrong speak at front grandparents-his Andi.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Terus gimana, dong? Aku pengin kamu ikut tampil.
lines.id: So what do we do? I want you to be up there.
lines.literal: then how, [dong]? I want you join appear.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Gimana kalau aku kasih sambutan singkat dari sahabat? Pakai bahasa Indonesia aja.
lines.id: How about I give a short speech as your best friend? In Indonesian.
lines.literal: how if I give speech short from close-friend? use language Indonesia just.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Wah, ide bagus! MC-nya biar Om Tono aja.
lines.id: Oh, great idea! Uncle Tono can do the MC bit.
lines.literal: wow, idea good! MC-the let Uncle Tono just.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Makasih udah ngerti, Rin. Aku jadi nggak enak nolak.
lines.id: Thanks for understanding, Rin. I feel bad saying no.
lines.literal: thanks already understand, Rin. I become not pleasant refuse.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Santai, Sar. Yang penting kamu ada di sana.
lines.id: Relax, Sar. What matters is that you're there.
lines.literal: relaxed, Sar. which important you exist at there.

notes: **Terharu banget, tapi…** — between close friends the refusal can be much more direct, but it still starts with warmth. Sarah thanks Rina with her feelings (*terharu*, moved) before she says anything else.
**Nggak pede** — *pede* is *PD*, *percaya diri*, “self-confident”, spelled the way it is said. Standard: *tidak percaya diri*. *Pede banget!* is “so full of himself!”.

**Bahasa Jawa halus** — Javanese has speech levels, and a wedding MC (*pranatacara* or *pembawa acara*) uses the most refined one (*krama*), full of ceremonial phrases. Even many Javanese people hire a professional for it, so Sarah's excuse is completely genuine.

**Eyang** is a respectful Javanese word for grandparent, used by families with a Central Javanese background — especially in Solo and Yogya. *Eyang-eyangnya Andi* means all of Andi's grandparents together.

**The counter-offer.** Sarah does not just say no; she offers something she *can* do (*Gimana kalau aku…?*). This is the most effective refusal strategy in Indonesian and it works just as well with bosses as with friends.

**Aku jadi nggak enak nolak** — “I end up feeling bad refusing”. *Jadi* here means “as a result, I become”. *Nolak* is the spoken form of *menolak*, to refuse; Rina's *pengin* is spoken *ingin*, and *makasih* is *terima kasih*.

grammars.title: Refusing a friend: the spoken forms
body: Between friends the same strategy — warmth, reason, counter-offer — is carried by everyday Jakarta Indonesian. Here are the spoken forms from Rina's call with their standard equivalents.
after: Notice how many of these are the nasal-only forms from A2 Unit 3: *ngobrol*, *ngomong*, *ngerti*, *nolak*. The *me-* prefix simply falls away in speech.
💬 *Santai* (“relaxed”) is the friend's way of saying “it's fine, don't worry”. Its written cousin in a message is *santai aja* or the slangy *santuy*.

sections.title: Nggak enak, sungkan, segan: a small dictionary of social discomfort

blocks.text: English has “awkward” and “embarrassed” and not much else. Indonesian has a whole family of words for the feelings that keep social life smooth. Learn to name them and you will understand a great deal of Indonesian behaviour.

head: Word
What you feel
Typical sentence
rows: too respectful or shy to ask or accept
reluctant out of respect or awe

blocks.text: *Jangan sungkan* (“don't hold back”) and *Anggap saja rumah sendiri* (“treat it as your own home”) are what good hosts say. They are sincere — and the polite guest still holds back a little.
The host's side of the ritual has its own phrases, and the guest's replies are just as fixed. You will hear this exchange at nearly every table you sit at:

items: *Ayo, dimakan, Mbak. Jangan malu-malu.* — Go on, eat, don't be shy.
*Tambah lagi, ya?* — Have some more? *Sudah, Bu, sudah cukup. Kenyang sekali.* — No really, that's plenty.
*Aduh, kok repot-repot, Bu?* — Oh, you shouldn't have gone to such trouble.
*Maaf merepotkan.* — Sorry to put you out. *Nggak repot, kok.* — It's no trouble at all.

sections.title: Hearing the no that sounds like a yes

blocks.text: The other half of the skill is recognising a refusal when it is aimed at you. None of these phrases is dishonest; they are simply how a no is delivered without damage.

head: What you hear
Literally
Often means
rows: yes, if nothing gets in the way, or a gentle no
I hear you, not I agree

blocks.title: If you really need a clear answer
items: Ask a closed, specific question: *Jadi hari Sabtu Bapak bisa atau tidak?*
Offer an easy way out: *Kalau tidak bisa, tidak apa-apa, lho.*
Ask a third person privately; they may tell you what the speaker could not.

blocks.text: *Insyaallah* (“God willing”) deserves special care. Among devout Muslims it is a sincere yes with humility attached; in everyday use it can also be a gentle no. Never tease anyone about it, and never assume which one you have heard — ask a friendly follow-up question if it matters.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
